```{r setup}
library(SurvFitSummary)
dat <- processing_dataset(
  system.file("extdata", "fit_example.csv", package = "SurvFitSummary"),
  column_arm = "TRT01P", column_survtime = "AVAL", column_cnsr = "CNSR",
  control_arm = "Control"
)
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
```

This vignette describes the models of `fit_survival_models()` and the tables
derived from them. The data are those of
`vignette("SurvFitSummary", package = "SurvFitSummary")`.

## Distributions

The parametric models are fitted with `flexsurv::flexsurvreg()`, with the
parameters of flexsurv. The default is the seven standard models of NICE DSU
Technical Support Document 14 (marked with *).

| Code | Model | Parameters (natural scale) | Location parameter |
|---|---|---|---|
| `"exp"` * | Exponential | rate | rate |
| `"weibull"` * | Weibull (accelerated failure time form) | shape, scale | scale |
| `"weibullPH"` | Weibull (proportional hazards form) | shape, scale | scale |
| `"rayleigh"` | Rayleigh (Weibull with shape 2) | scale | scale |
| `"lnorm"` * | Lognormal | meanlog, sdlog | meanlog |
| `"llogis"` * | Log-logistic | shape, scale | scale |
| `"gompertz"` * | Gompertz | shape, rate | rate |
| `"gamma"` * | Gamma | shape, rate | rate |
| `"gengamma"` * | Generalized gamma (Prentice 1974) | mu, sigma, Q | mu |
| `"gengamma.orig"` | Generalized gamma (Stacy 1962) | shape, scale, k | scale |
| `"genf"` | Generalized F (Prentice 1975) | mu, sigma, Q, P | mu |
| `"genf.orig"` | Generalized F (original form) | mu, sigma, s1, s2 | mu |

The spline models of Royston and Parmar (2002) are fitted with
`flexsurv::flexsurvspline()`. They model the log cumulative hazard (scale
`"hazard"`), the log cumulative odds (`"odds"`) or the probit of the survival
(`"normal"`) as a natural cubic spline of log time with parameters `gamma0`,
`gamma1`, ...; without internal knots they reduce to the Weibull,
log-logistic and lognormal models. The boundary knots are the smallest and
largest log event times, and the internal knots are by default at equally
spaced quantiles of the log event times.

## Independent and dependent fits

Each arm is fitted separately (`fit_type = "independent"`), and the arms are
fitted together with the arm as a covariate of the location parameter on its
transformed scale (`fit_type = "dependent"`, labelled `"Both arms"`); for the
spline models the arm shifts `gamma0`.

```{r fit}
fits <- fit_survival_models(dat, distributions = c("weibull", "llogis"),
                            spline_scales = "hazard", spline_knots = 1:2)
par <- parameter_table(fits)
par[par$fit_type == "dependent" & par$model == "Weibull", ]
```

```{r effect, include = FALSE}
b <- par[par$fit_type == "dependent" & par$model == "Weibull" &
           par$parameter == "ARMTreatment" & par$scale == "transformed", ]
```

In the dependent Weibull model the treatment multiplies the scale, that is
the time to any given survival, by exp(`r f3(b$est)`) = `r f2(exp(b$est))`
(95% CI `r f2(exp(b$lcl))` to `r f2(exp(b$ucl))`). The natural scale is that
of flexsurv; on the transformed scale the positive parameters are on the log
scale, which is the scale of the covariance matrices and of the simulations
below.

## Knots of the spline models

`spline_knot_table()` gives the internal knots of each fit with the number
at risk and the Kaplan-Meier estimate at each knot, which shows how much
data supports each part of the spline.

```{r knots}
spline_knot_table(fits)
```

Knots can also be given on the time scale, one vector per spline model; the
vectors must have different numbers of knots, and the knots must lie between
the smallest and largest event times of every fit.

```{r user-knots}
fits_knots <- fit_survival_models(dat, distributions = NULL,
                                  spline_scales = "odds",
                                  knots = list(12, c(6, 18)))
gof_table(fits_knots)
```

## Covariance matrices and Cholesky factors

The covariance matrix of the estimates and its lower triangular Cholesky
factor L, with L L' equal to the covariance matrix, are given on the
transformed and natural scales. A probabilistic sensitivity analysis draws
parameter vectors as the estimate plus L z, with z standard normal, on the
transformed scale.

```{r cholesky}
covariance_table(fits, scale = "transformed")[1:4, ]
chol <- covariance_table(fits, type = "cholesky", scale = "transformed")
rows <- chol$fit_type == "independent" & chol$arm == "Control" &
  chol$model == "Weibull"
L <- matrix(chol$value[rows], nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
            dimnames = list(unique(chol$row[rows]), unique(chol$col[rows])))
L
est <- par[par$fit_type == "independent" & par$arm == "Control" &
             par$model == "Weibull" & par$scale == "transformed", ]
mu <- est$est[match(rownames(L), est$parameter)]
set.seed(1)
draws <- mu + L %*% matrix(stats::rnorm(2 * 10000), nrow = 2)
# Natural scale: shape and scale
summary(t(exp(draws)))
```

```{r cholesky-values, include = FALSE}
v <- covariance_table(fits, scale = "transformed")
v <- v[v$fit_type == "independent" & v$arm == "Control" &
         v$model == "Weibull", ]
```

The variances of the 10000 draws, `r f3(1e3 * stats::var(draws[1, ]))` and
`r f3(1e3 * stats::var(draws[2, ]))` (times 1000), reproduce those of the
covariance matrix, `r f3(1e3 * v$value[v$row == v$col][1])` and
`r f3(1e3 * v$value[v$row == v$col][2])`.

## Predictions with confidence intervals

`predict_survival()` gives the survival, the hazard or the cumulative hazard
of each model. With `conf_int = TRUE` the confidence limits are the
quantiles of the predictions for `n_sim` parameter vectors drawn from the
asymptotic normal distribution of the estimates; the seed is set for each
model and arm, so that the limits do not depend on the other models, and the
random number generator of the session is left unchanged.

```{r predict}
pred <- predict_survival(fits, times = c(12, 60), conf_int = TRUE)
pred[pred$fit_type == "independent" & pred$arm == "Control", ]
```

```{r predict-values, include = FALSE}
w5 <- pred[pred$fit_type == "independent" & pred$arm == "Control" &
             pred$model == "Weibull" & pred$time == 60, ]
```

The Weibull model of the control arm predicts a survival of `r f3(w5$est)`
at 5 years (95% CI `r f3(w5$lcl)` to `r f3(w5$ucl)`).
`survival_summary()` gives the median, the mean and the restricted mean
survival up to a time horizon.

```{r summary}
survival_summary(fits, time_horizon = 60)
```

```{r ci-plot, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_survival_fits(fits, models = "Weibull", fit_type = "dependent",
                   conf_int = TRUE, time_horizon = 120)
```

## Comparing the models

`gof_table()` gives the log-likelihood, AIC and BIC of each model, sorted by
AIC within each fit; the number of patients is used for the BIC. The fit
statistics compare the models within the follow-up only, so that the
plausibility of the extrapolation is judged separately, for example from the
hazard functions and from external data.

```{r gof}
gof_table(fits)
```

## Models that fail

A model that fails or warns does not stop the others: its status (`"ok"`,
`"warning"` or `"error"`) and message are kept in `fits$models`, printed by
`print()`, written to the sheet "Model status" of the workbook and listed in
the report.

```{r status}
fits$models[, c("fit_type", "arm", "model", "status", "message")]
```

The likelihood is maximised by `stats::optim()` (BFGS) with the settings in
`control`; the default tolerance (`reltol = 1e-10`) is smaller than that of
`optim()`. flexsurv has no analytic gradient for the spline models on the
normal scale, for which the step of the numerical gradient is `ndeps = 1e-5`
unless `control` sets it.

## Colours, line types and text sizes of the plots

The plots take the colours and line types of the arms, curves or elements
they draw in `colours` and `linetypes`, and font sizes in points in
`text_sizes`. A named vector changes the entries it names and the others
keep their defaults; an unnamed vector gives one value per entry, in the
order of the legend. For the fitted curves of one arm, the names are the
labels of the models and `"Kaplan-Meier"` (or `"Smoothed empirical hazard"`
in `plot_hazard_fits()`).

```{r appearance, fig.height = 7}
plot_survival_fits(fits, arms = "Control", time_horizon = 120,
                   colours = c("Kaplan-Meier" = "grey40",
                               "Weibull" = "#009E73"),
                   linetypes = c("Hazards, 1 knot" = "dashed",
                                 "Hazards, 2 knots" = "dotted"),
                   text_sizes = c(axis_title = 16, legend = 12))
```

## References

Latimer NR (2011, updated 2013). NICE DSU Technical Support Document 14:
Survival analysis for economic evaluations alongside clinical trials -
extrapolation with patient-level data.

Royston P, Parmar MKB (2002). Flexible parametric proportional-hazards and
proportional-odds models for censored survival data, with application to
prognostic modelling and estimation of treatment effects. Statistics in
Medicine 21(15):2175-2197.
